name: Grace Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the practice administrator at Kingsway Dental, which has four dentists, three dental nurses and a hygienist. I run the appointment book, send the six-month check-up reminders, file the patient records, and do the insurance claims, which are the worst bit. On a good day the book is full and nobody's waiting more than ten minutes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bad day is when Dr Shah is off sick and I have to ring twenty-two patients before nine to move them. People take it personally, like I've cancelled their birthday. I use the AI tool on the practice software now and then, mainly to draft the reminder letters, once I'd seen the other practice in town using it without disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Then it's basically the tool I already use for the letters, and not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for the letters and that's it. I'd probably tell my partner Tom that all the fuss was about a fancy spellchecker. I don't really post opinions online; I mostly post our cat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. People always need their teeth done, and someone has to deal with the patients who want a Saturday appointment that doesn't exist. The only thing I'd watch is the practice owner, Dr Morris, who talks about retiring and selling to one of the big dental chains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep using the letter tool. Tom and I put about £200 a month into savings, and we'd keep doing that. I'd maybe ask about the dental nurse training the practice sometimes pays for, just because I've been curious about it for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bored of the hype, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Dr Morris sells to a chain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chains have a central booking team in another city, so the front desk often shrinks to one person. I've seen it happen. My friend Kemi's dental practice was bought by a chain, and three admin became one in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dental nurse training, if you're fine where you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like the clinical side when I see it, and it's more money after a couple of years. It's not a plan to escape, more a door I keep looking at.

say: The tool is handy for **letters**, and that's it.
All the fuss was about a **fancy spellchecker**, I'd tell Tom at dinner.
think: People always need **teeth done**, so my job feels safe.
The real watch point is Dr Morris **selling to a chain**.
do: Keep using the **letter tool** and doing the job.
Keep saving **£200 a month** with Tom.
Ask about the **dental nurse training** the practice sometimes funds.
S0.quote: My friend Kemi's dental practice was bought by a chain, and three admin became one in a year.
fieldNote: She feels **secure** because the practice is busy and dentistry is local.
Her one worry is a **sale to a chain**, which she's seen cut admin jobs.
The dental nurse idea is **curiosity**, not fear, at this stage.

steps.text: Keep drafting reminder letters with the practice's AI tool
Ask Dr Morris about funded dental nurse training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Booking and answering patients. That's literally my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change front desks a lot, and that practices should be honest with staff about it. At work I'd be fairly upbeat, because the dentists don't like a gloomy reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the practice goes from two of us on reception to one, plus a booking system that answers the phone at night. Mandy, the other receptionist, has been there fifteen years and the patients love her, so I'd assume I'm the one who's moved or cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dr Morris for the dental nurse training this year rather than someday, and offer to work reception part-time while I do it. I'd learn the new booking system properly, because whoever knows it best looks useful. And Tom and I would push savings from about four months to six before booking any holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think dental nursing is safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's hands-on: suction, passing instruments, calming a nervous patient in the chair. The card says robots spread there more slowly, and I've never seen a robot hold a crying ten-year-old's hand in the dentist's chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mandy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn the system too, and I'd show her. I'm not going to compete with her by keeping things to myself.

say: Front desks will **change a lot**, and practices should be honest with staff.
I'd stay **upbeat at work**, because dentists don't like a gloomy reception.
think: Reception goes from **two to one**, plus a night booking system.
Mandy's **fifteen years** mean I'm the one moved or cut.
do: Ask for **dental nurse training** this year, working reception part-time.
Build savings to **six months** before booking a holiday.
feel: Anxious, but in a way she can **act on**.
S1.quote: I've never seen a robot hold a crying ten-year-old's hand in the dentist's chair.
fieldNote: She expects **her post** to be the one cut, not her colleague's.
She moves towards **hands-on nursing**, matching the slower robot timeline.
She chooses to **help a rival** rather than compete, which says a lot.

steps.text: Start funded dental nurse training while working reception part-time
Learn the new booking system before anyone else
Build savings to six months before booking a holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And then robots in 2031. Okay. Give me a second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, quickly, because millions of desk jobs going at once isn't something families can sort out on their own. At work I'd still try to be calm for the patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, reception is gone by 2028, because an AI does every phone call, booking and claim better than me and never takes holidays. The only thing that buys me time is the three years before robots, if I'm already in the surgery as a nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the dental nurse course immediately, even if it means a pay cut while training, which would be maybe £300 a month less. We'd stop saving for a house and just keep the cushion. Tom's an electrician, so he'd probably be okay for a few more years, and I'd lean on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I'm running for a bus that's already pulling away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe patients still want a person in the room. Maybe not. I'd be 32 and I'd have to work that out then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None, hopefully. We'd cut the car down to one, because Tom needs the van anyway, and we'd stop eating out.

say: The government needs a **quick plan**, because families can't fix this alone.
I'd stay **calm for patients** at work.
think: Reception is **gone by 2028**: calls, bookings and claims.
The **three years** before robots help only if I'm already nursing.
do: Start the **dental nurse course** now, even on about £300 less.
Stop **house savings** and keep the cushion.
Sell **my car** and share Tom's van.
feel: **Alarmed**, like chasing a bus that's already leaving.
S2.quote: Reception is gone by 2028, because an AI does every phone call, booking and claim better than me and never takes holidays.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the reception job** and acts fast anyway.
She uses the **robot delay** directly, moving into the surgery.
Her partner's **electrician work** is the household's short-term buffer.

steps.text: Start the dental nurse course now, taking a pay cut
Stop saving for a house and keep the cushion
Sell her car and share Tom's van
Lean on Tom's electrician income for a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels more like a plan than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people start now. I'd tell my friends at other practices to look at the training options early, before everyone wants them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep my job for two or three years and then it's gone or part-time. That's actually enough to qualify as a dental nurse while still earning. I'm not excited, but I'm not lost either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask Dr Morris to put me on the nurse training and pay half, which he's done for others. I'd keep working reception on the days I'm not training. We'd keep saving for a house, slower, about £100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. More like a to-do list than a fright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Dr Morris says no to paying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay it myself, it's about £1,500 I think. That's most of one month's savings. Paying £1,500 for dental nurse training hurts, but it's an investment, not a holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the practice would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mandy. She's 52 and she's been the voice of Kingsway Dental on the phone for fifteen years. Five years would take her close to retirement, but not quite there.

say: Five years is **enough to prepare** if people start now.
I'd tell friends to look at **training early**, before everyone wants it.
think: I keep my job **two or three years**, then it goes part-time or ends.
That's enough to **qualify as a nurse** while still earning.
do: Ask Dr Morris to **pay half** of the nurse training.
Keep saving for a house at about **£100 a month**.
feel: Anxious but **steady**, like a to-do list.
S3.quote: Paying £1,500 for dental nurse training hurts, but it's an investment, not a holiday.
fieldNote: She still expects her **reception job to shrink**, so she stays anxious.
She treats the training cost as an **investment**, not a loss.
Her concern for **Mandy** shows she thinks about the older staff.

steps.text: Ask Dr Morris to pay half the dental nurse training
Work reception on the days without training
Save £100 a month towards a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, I can actually breathe with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, and there's no excuse for not getting ready. I'd probably say it to Tom's brothers, who think AI is only a problem for people in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine if I do the nurse training in the next couple of years. The reception job still shrinks earlier than 2036, maybe 2030, because the booking systems are already good. But I'd be in the surgery by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep reception going and start the nurse course in the autumn. Tom and I would buy a small house in the next year or two, while both our incomes look solid to a bank. Maybe we'd plan a baby after I've qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly okay. I'm a planner, and ten years is plannable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tom's brothers think it's an office problem. Are they right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. They've got about three years longer than me, according to the card. But someone still has to plan their jobs and send the invoices, and that's thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still have a baby in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. My mum had me during a recession and says it never felt like the wrong time. I'd just want to be qualified first.

say: Ten years is a **fair run-up**, with no excuse not to get ready.
AI isn't only an **office problem**, I'd tell Tom's brothers.
think: I'd be **fine** if I train as a nurse in the next two years.
do: Start the **nurse course** in the autumn while keeping reception.
Buy a **small house** with Tom in a year or two.
feel: Uneasy but mostly okay; ten years is **plannable**.
S4.quote: I'm a planner, and ten years is plannable.
fieldNote: With a decade she sees a **clear route** into nursing, so worry drops.
She still dates the reception job's end to **around 2030**.
Family plans continue, just **sequenced** after qualifying.

steps.text: Start the dental nurse course in the autumn
Buy a small house with Tom in a year or two
Plan a baby after qualifying as a dental nurse

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to train while still earning. What would help is funded training for jobs like dental nursing, and a bit of income support while people do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about patients. Older patients ring the practice just to hear a friendly voice before an appointment they're scared of. Somebody should decide whether that matters before it disappears.

headlineQuote: Older patients ring the practice just to hear a friendly voice before an appointment they're scared of.
portrait: Grace, 27, is practice administrator at **Kingsway Dental** and lives with Tom, an electrician.
She uses the practice's AI tool **now and then**, once she's seen it work elsewhere.
In the quiet picture she feels **secure**, watching only for a sale to a dental chain.
In every faster picture she expects reception to shrink and moves into **dental nursing**, which is hands-on.
She's a **planner**: house, baby and training all come in an order she can manage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to train while still earning.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded training** for hands-on jobs like dental nursing.
